title: What is Terminal Value?
subtitle: The single largest share of value in most DCF models
openingQuestion: A DCF model forecasts detailed cash flow for 5 years. So how is the company's value from year 6 onward (forever) handled?
openingOptions: It is estimated using Terminal Value - a value representing all cash flow from year 6 to infinity, discounted back to present value at the end of the forecast period and added to the total DCF value
It is calculated using only the book value of current assets
Terminal Value is always zero because the distant future is uncertain
It is ignored entirely because it's too far out to forecast accurately
explanation: Since it's impossible to forecast cash flow in detail forever, a DCF model typically forecasts in detail for 5-10 years, then calculates a Terminal Value representing all remaining value after that. Terminal Value usually accounts for 60-80% of the total DCF value - it is the most SENSITIVE and important part of the entire model, even though it sits in the 'most distant future'.

diagram.label: Forecast in detail through the final year
Everything after is bundled into terminal value

realWorldExample.company: The sensitivity of a DCF model
realWorldExample.description: A small change in the long-term growth assumption (from 2% to 3%) can shift Terminal Value - and therefore the total DCF value - by tens of percent, illustrating how extremely sensitive this part of the model is.

quiz.question: Why do analysts always recommend running a particularly careful sensitivity analysis on Terminal Value?
options: Because it accounts for most of the value while resting on the most distant assumptions
Because it's the only part of the model not discounted back to today's value
Because valuation standards require sensitivity disclosure for this part specifically
Because it's calculated with a different formula than the detailed forecast part
quiz.explanation: Because Terminal Value accounts for most of the total DCF value, and is calculated using long-term assumptions that are hard to forecast accurately (perpetual growth, future cost of capital), small errors in these assumptions get amplified into large errors in the final result - this is why sensitivity analysis is mandatory, not optional, when presenting DCF results.

quiz.question: If an analyst deliberately shortens the explicit forecast period to just 2 years instead of the usual 5-10 years before calculating Terminal Value, what could happen to the reliability of the valuation result?
options: The result becomes more reliable because fewer forecast years mean less error
Terminal Value takes up a larger share, making the result less reliable
No effect at all, because the total value stays the same
The model simply cannot run if the forecast is under three years
quiz.explanation: Shortening the explicit forecast period doesn't solve the uncertainty of the future - it just shifts the forecasting burden onto Terminal Value SOONER, making the final result depend more heavily on the least certain long-term assumptions. This is why analysts usually choose a forecast period long enough for the company to reach a stable growth state before applying Terminal Value.

quiz.question: Final-year cash flow is 100 billion, WACC is 10%, perpetual growth is 3%. What is the Terminal Value?
options: 3,333 billion (= 100 ÷ 0.03, mistakenly dividing by g)
1,000 billion (= 100 ÷ 0.10, forgetting growth)
769 billion (= 100 ÷ (0.10 + 0.03), adding instead of subtracting)
quiz.explanation: TV = next year's CF / (r - g) = 103 / 0.07 ≈ 1,429 billion. The denominator is only 7%, so it's highly sensitive: raising g to 4% pushes the result to 1,717 billion, a 20% increase from one assumption alone.

quiz.question: What are the two common methods for calculating Terminal Value?
options: Industry average and the company's own historical average
Discounted cash flow and comparable company analysis
Book value and asset liquidation value
Gordon Growth and Exit Multiple, run both
quiz.explanation: One is based on pure theoretical perpetual growth, the other anchors to a real market multiple. Running both and comparing is the standard cross-check in the industry.

quiz.question: Terminal Value accounts for 85% of the model's value. How should one respond?
options: Review the long-term assumptions and extend the forecast period
Accept it, since that share falls within a normal range
Drop Terminal Value and use only the detailed forecast part
Raise the discount rate to pull that share down to a reasonable level
quiz.explanation: Going far beyond the usual 60-80% range means almost the entire conclusion rests on guesswork. The fix is to forecast in detail for longer, shifting more value into the better-grounded portion of the model.

keyTakeaways: Terminal Value: the value representing cash flow from after the explicit forecast period to infinity
Usually accounts for 60-80% of total DCF value - the most sensitive part of the model
Requires careful sensitivity analysis because of its enormous impact on the final result

practicePrompt.question: A DCF model forecasts the company's cash flow in detail for the next 5 years, but the company keeps operating indefinitely after that. How does the DCF model account for the value of all cash flow after year 5 without forecasting in detail to infinity?
options: The DCF model simply ignores all value after year 5 because it can't be forecast accurately that far out
Terminal Value: the value of cash flow from after the explicit forecast period to infinity
The DCF model assumes the company will fully cease operations right after year 5
Terminal Value is only a theoretical concept, not actually calculated in real DCF models
practicePrompt.explanation: Terminal Value: the value representing cash flow from after the explicit forecast period to infinity. Since detailed forecasting forever is impossible, a DCF model uses a formula (Gordon Growth or Exit Multiple) to condense all distant future value into a single number - Terminal Value usually accounts for 60-80% of total DCF value.

summary.keyIdea: Terminal Value: the value representing cash flow from after the explicit forecast period to infinity
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a definition to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Think about one of your own long-term decisions (buying a home, choosing a career) - does the 'value' lie in the next 5 years, or in the rest of your life after that? That's the intuition behind Terminal Value.
application.secondary: Terminal Value dominates DCF value the same way the rest of your life dominates your total lifespan beyond the next 5 years.

sections.text: A surprising fact for many new to DCF: the largest share of the entire valuation usually doesn't come from the 5-10 years of detailed forecast, but from a single number representing 'everything after that' - Terminal Value.

It's impossible to forecast a company's cash flow in detail forever, so a DCF model typically forecasts in detail for 5-10 years, then calculates a Terminal Value representing all remaining value after that - from the final forecast year to infinity. Notably: Terminal Value usually accounts for 60-80% of total DCF value, despite sitting in the 'most distant future' and hardest-to-forecast part of the model.

A small change in the long-term growth assumption - say from 2% to 3% - can shift Terminal Value, and therefore total DCF value, by tens of percent. This is why sensitivity analysis on Terminal Value is mandatory, not optional. A common mistake is shortening the explicit forecast period (for example, just 2 years instead of 5-10) to 'simplify' the model - but this doesn't solve the uncertainty of the future, it just shifts the forecasting burden onto Terminal Value SOONER, making the result depend more heavily on the least certain long-term assumptions.

items: Terminal Value represents cash flow from after the explicit forecast period to infinity
Usually accounts for 60-80% of total DCF value - the most important part, not a 'side' part
Choose a forecast period long enough for the company to reach a stable growth state before calculating Terminal Value
Two common calculation methods: the Gordon Growth Method and the Exit Multiple Method

lines: If Terminal Value accounts for most of the DCF value, then scrutinising the assumptions behind it matters more than any other line in the model.
